title: Polynomial constraints, exceptions and proof
subject: Mathematics
scope_summary: Advanced competition extension around real one-variable polynomials. No calculus or complex-number prerequisite.

microtopics.title: What finite polynomial data actually determine
microtopics.badge_reason: Requires preserving constraints across multiple inferential steps rather than a single routine manipulation.
entry_assumptions: Can factor routine one-variable polynomials and use the factor theorem.
Can distinguish a stated domain/degree bound from an inferred property.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Finite agreement becomes an identity only after a structural bound makes too many distinct roots impossible for the difference polynomial.

teaching_path.action: Separate observed values from structural assumptions such as degree, parity or domain.
teaching_path.why_valid: A conclusion is licensed only by the conditions actually stated.
teaching_path.output: A constraint ledger that distinguishes observations from bounds.

teaching_path.action: Replace agreement of two polynomials by zeros of their difference.
teaching_path.why_valid: p(c)=q(c) exactly means (p-q)(c)=0.
teaching_path.output: Finite agreement becomes a root statement about one polynomial.

teaching_path.action: Compare the number of distinct forced roots with the allowed degree of the difference.
teaching_path.why_valid: A nonzero degree-n polynomial has at most n distinct real roots.
teaching_path.output: Either identity is forced or a nonzero vanishing factor remains possible.

teaching_path.action: When a bound is removed, explicitly parameterize the vanishing-factor family instead of retaining the bounded conclusion.
teaching_path.why_valid: The factor theorem characterizes every polynomial difference sharing the observed zeros.
teaching_path.output: A bounded inference and its unbounded family are kept distinct.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Three matching inputs prove two unrestricted polynomials are identical.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Two unrestricted polynomials agree at x=0,1,2. Must they be identical?
misconceptions.repair: No. Their difference may be x(x-1)(x-2)h(x). Identity follows only when an applicable degree bound makes that many distinct roots impossible.

exit_task.prompt: Two real polynomials of degree at most 2 agree at three distinct inputs. State what follows and what fails if the degree bound is removed.

answer.summary: With the degree bound they are identical. Without it, their difference may be the three-node product times an arbitrary real polynomial.
reasoning: No. Their difference may be x(x-1)(x-2)h(x). Identity follows only when an applicable degree bound makes that many distinct roots impossible.

microtopics.title: Multiplicity, sign and exact real-zero sets
microtopics.badge_reason: Requires preserving constraints across multiple inferential steps rather than a single routine manipulation.
entry_assumptions: Can factor routine one-variable polynomials and use the factor theorem.
Can distinguish a stated domain/degree bound from an inferred property.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Local sign behaviour determines only the parity of a root's multiplicity; the degree budget and other constraints are what turn those parities into exact multiplicities.

teaching_path.action: At each stated zero, record whether the polynomial changes sign or keeps the same nonzero sign locally.
teaching_path.why_valid: The local sign condition is evidence about multiplicity parity, not about scale.
teaching_path.output: Odd/even parity requirements at each zero.

teaching_path.action: Assign the least positive multiplicities with those parities, then compare their sum with the degree bound.
teaching_path.why_valid: Each multiplicity contributes to total degree.
teaching_path.output: The remaining degree budget, if any.

teaching_path.action: Add monicity/value constraints and account for any residual factor that the degree budget permits.
teaching_path.why_valid: Residual factors may introduce forbidden real zeros even when the named factors are correct.
teaching_path.output: A finite candidate list or a unique factorization.

teaching_path.action: Check sign behaviour, exact zero set and every value/leading-coefficient condition separately.
teaching_path.why_valid: Correct factors alone do not prove completeness.
teaching_path.output: Verified multiplicities and no omitted real-zero source.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Every named zero is simple unless the stem explicitly says repeated.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If a continuous polynomial has the same nonzero sign immediately to both sides of a zero, can that zero be simple?
misconceptions.repair: No. A simple (odd-multiplicity) root changes sign. Same-sign crossing data require even multiplicity.

exit_task.prompt: A degree-at-most-4 polynomial has zeros -1,0,1, changes sign at ±1 and not at 0. What multiplicity pattern is forced?

reasoning: No. A simple (odd-multiplicity) root changes sign. Same-sign crossing data require even multiplicity.

microtopics.title: Proving a least degree under an exact zero-set constraint
microtopics.badge_reason: Requires preserving constraints across multiple inferential steps rather than a single routine manipulation.
entry_assumptions: Can factor routine one-variable polynomials and use the factor theorem.
Can distinguish a stated domain/degree bound from an inferred property.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A construction proves possibility only; minimality needs a lower-bound argument that eliminates every smaller degree while respecting the exact real-zero set.

teaching_path.action: Factor all required zeros first and translate the remaining value constraints to an auxiliary polynomial.
teaching_path.why_valid: This isolates where extra roots could appear.
teaching_path.output: An auxiliary factor with explicit value/sign constraints.

teaching_path.action: Turn each proposed total degree into a maximum degree for the auxiliary factor.
teaching_path.why_valid: The required factors already consume part of the degree.
teaching_path.output: A finite sequence of smaller-degree cases to eliminate.

teaching_path.action: Use value equations, continuity and quadratic discriminant/sign facts to show why each smaller auxiliary degree creates a contradiction or an extra real zero.
teaching_path.why_valid: Those tools address the exact-zero-set condition, not merely interpolation.
teaching_path.output: A genuine lower bound on total degree.

teaching_path.action: Only after the lower bound is closed, build one polynomial at that degree and check that any remaining factor has no additional real zeros.
teaching_path.why_valid: Possibility plus the lower bound proves minimality.
teaching_path.output: A minimal-degree witness with exact zero set.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Once a low-degree example is found, no separate proof that smaller degrees fail is needed.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If you exhibit a degree-5 polynomial satisfying all conditions, have you proved 5 is least?
misconceptions.repair: No. You must eliminate degrees below 5. The exact-zero-set condition often makes continuity or discriminant arguments the missing lower-bound step.

exit_task.prompt: Explain the two obligations in any least-degree polynomial problem with an exact real-zero set.

answer.summary: Prove every smaller degree impossible, then exhibit and verify one polynomial at the first remaining degree.
reasoning: No. You must eliminate degrees below 5. The exact-zero-set condition often makes continuity or discriminant arguments the missing lower-bound step.
answer.check: Apply the statement to a fresh changed case and verify the relevant condition explicitly.

independent_checks.statement: CHECK: Separate the two obligations in a least-degree claim: rule out every smaller degree, then verify one witness.
APPLY: If an auxiliary quadratic has opposite signs at two inputs, use continuity and multiplicity to decide whether a lone double root could account for the sign change.
CONNECT: Relate the same residual-factor check to proving that an exact real-zero-set classification has omitted no polynomial.

CU-MATH-ISS52-PARAMETER-1.stem: For G_t(x)=x(x+3)((t-2)x^2+(t+1)), derive every parameter value at which the degree or distinct real-zero pattern can change, then classify the parameter line.

answer.summary: Critical values are t=-1, 17/10, 2. For t<-1 and t>2 there are two distinct simple real zeros 0,-3. At t=-1 there are two distinct zeros with 0 of multiplicity 3. For -1<t<2 except 17/10 there are four distinct simple zeros. At t=17/10 there are three distinct zeros with -3 double. At t=2 the polynomial drops to degree 2 with simple zeros 0,-3.
reasoning: Factorization is already exposed. Degree drops when t-2=0. Extra real roots require (t+1)/(2-t)>0, with boundary t=-1. Collision with -3 occurs when (t+1)/(2-t)=9, giving t=17/10. Order the events and test each interval; refactor at each event.
answer.check: Choose t=0, t=19/10 and t=3 as interval checks, then substitute each exceptional t directly.

microtopics.title: Exhaustive parameter case splits from structural events
microtopics.badge_reason: Requires an exhaustive event set before any interval sampling; isolated collisions and degree drops are easy to omit.
entry_assumptions: Can factor routine one-variable polynomials and use the factor theorem.
Can distinguish a stated domain/degree bound from an inferred property.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Do not start by sampling parameter values. First derive every equality or sign boundary at which degree, root existence or root coincidence can change; those events determine the exhaustive case split.

teaching_path.action: Factor the family into fixed-root factors and parameter-dependent factors.
teaching_path.why_valid: A factored form exposes which structural features can change with the parameter.
teaching_path.output: Fixed roots and a parameter-dependent root condition.

teaching_path.action: List event types before solving cases: leading-coefficient zero, real-root existence boundary, and collision with an existing root.
teaching_path.why_valid: Away from such events, the algebraic root pattern cannot change continuously without crossing one of these boundaries.
teaching_path.output: A complete checklist of event equations.

teaching_path.action: Solve every event equation and order the resulting parameter values.
teaching_path.why_valid: The ordered event set partitions the line into points and open intervals with stable structural conditions.
teaching_path.output: An ordered critical-value set and interval partition.

teaching_path.action: Classify one sample in each open interval and refactor exactly at each event point to read multiplicities.
teaching_path.why_valid: Interval stability plus direct event-point checks makes the classification exhaustive.
teaching_path.output: A complete degree/root/multiplicity table.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Testing several convenient parameter values is enough to claim a complete classification.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A table covers t<-1 and t>-1 but never solves when an extra root collides with a fixed root. Is it exhaustive?
misconceptions.repair: No. Collision values can be isolated inside an interval and change the distinct-root count without changing a sign condition. Derive collision equations explicitly.

exit_task.prompt: For H_s=x(x+1)((s-3)x^2+(s+2)), name the three event types you must derive before splitting cases; do not solve them.

answer.summary: Degree drop, real-root existence boundary, and collision of an extra root with a fixed root.
reasoning: No. Collision values can be isolated inside an interval and change the distinct-root count without changing a sign condition. Derive collision equations explicitly.
answer.check: Apply the statement to a fresh changed case and verify the relevant condition explicitly.

microtopics.title: Geometry-derived models versus finite interpolation
microtopics.badge_reason: Requires preserving constraints across multiple inferential steps rather than a single routine manipulation.
entry_assumptions: Can factor routine one-variable polynomials and use the factor theorem.
Can distinguish a stated domain/degree bound from an inferred property.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Matching a finite table is evidence of agreement at those inputs, not a license to replace a model derived from the mechanism and its domain.

teaching_path.action: Write the physical dimensions and derive the model from the construction before fitting any formula.
teaching_path.why_valid: The mechanism determines how the quantity depends on the input.
teaching_path.output: A geometry-derived formula.

teaching_path.action: Derive the admissible domain from positive physical dimensions and keep limiting configurations separate.
teaching_path.why_valid: A formula outside the physical domain is not a box model there.
teaching_path.output: A declared physical domain.

teaching_path.action: Compare a competing fit with the derived model by subtracting formulas or using a new admissible input.
teaching_path.why_valid: Finite matching nodes can be factored out of the difference.
teaching_path.output: A discriminating test away from the recorded rows.

teaching_path.action: Check physical invariants such as nonnegative volume and boundary behaviour.
teaching_path.why_valid: A candidate that violates a required physical property cannot be the governing model.
teaching_path.output: A model verdict supported by mechanism and domain.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A polynomial that matches every row in a short exact table must be the underlying physical model.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Two formulas agree at three admissible inputs. Without a degree/structure assumption, does that prove they agree everywhere?
misconceptions.repair: No. Derive the model from the mechanism or impose a justified structural bound; otherwise a nonzero polynomial can vanish at all sampled inputs.

exit_task.prompt: State one reason a three-point fit can fail as a physical model even when all three rows are exact.

answer.summary: Finite agreement does not encode the mechanism or domain; another polynomial can share those three values and differ elsewhere.
reasoning: No. Derive the model from the mechanism or impose a justified structural bound; otherwise a nonzero polynomial can vanish at all sampled inputs.

microtopics.title: Cancellation, original domains and polynomial extensions
microtopics.badge_reason: Requires preserving constraints across multiple inferential steps rather than a single routine manipulation.
entry_assumptions: Can factor routine one-variable polynomials and use the factor theorem.
Can distinguish a stated domain/degree bound from an inferred property.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Cancelling a common factor simplifies the rule only where the cancelled denominator was nonzero; assigning a value at the hole is a separate extension operation.

teaching_path.action: Record the original domain before simplifying a rational expression.
teaching_path.why_valid: A function includes both a rule and its admissible inputs.
teaching_path.output: An explicit excluded-value set.

teaching_path.action: Factor and cancel only under the nonzero condition already recorded.
teaching_path.why_valid: Algebraic cancellation is valid where the cancelled factor is nonzero.
teaching_path.output: A simpler rule with the original domain unchanged.

teaching_path.action: Classify zeros by requiring both rule value zero and membership in the original domain.
teaching_path.why_valid: An excluded input cannot be a zero of a function that is undefined there.
teaching_path.output: The original function's zero set.

teaching_path.action: Describe any all-real polynomial with the same rule as an extension, and say exactly what new value it supplies.
teaching_path.why_valid: Extension changes the domain intentionally rather than retroactively changing the original function.
teaching_path.output: Original function and polynomial extension kept distinct.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: After cancellation, the excluded point automatically returns to the function's domain.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If (x-c) cancels and the simplified formula is zero at x=c, is c automatically a zero of the original rational function?
misconceptions.repair: No. Check the original domain first. The simplified polynomial can define an extension, but that is a different function.

exit_task.prompt: Complete the sentence: cancelling a common factor preserves ___ but does not automatically preserve ___.

answer.summary: It preserves the values on the original domain; it does not automatically enlarge that domain.
reasoning: No. Check the original domain first. The simplified polynomial can define an extension, but that is a different function.

microtopics.title: Qualified rules instead of unconditional polynomial slogans
microtopics.badge_reason: The learner must identify which hidden hypothesis belongs to each superficially familiar rule and preserve it across mixed examples.
entry_assumptions: Can factor routine polynomials and read a declared domain or degree bound.
microtopics.inferential_jump: The decisive move is not more algebra; it is attaching the correct hypothesis to each inference before executing it.

teaching_path.action: Rewrite every shortcut as a conditional statement before applying it.
teaching_path.why_valid: A mathematical rule is only valid on the domain and under the structural hypotheses that justify its inference.
teaching_path.output: A condition ledger for cancellation, degree, real-root count and finite-data identity.

teaching_path.action: For cancellation and degree, check original-domain exclusions, simplification, and parameter values that may kill the leading coefficient.
teaching_path.why_valid: Cancellation is division under a nonzero condition, and degree depends on the first nonzero coefficient after simplification.
teaching_path.output: Qualified domain and degree rules.

teaching_path.action: For roots and finite agreement, convert the claim to a root count for a nonzero polynomial or difference polynomial.
teaching_path.why_valid: The root-count theorem is an upper bound for nonzero polynomials, and identity from finite agreement needs a degree bound on the difference.
teaching_path.output: Qualified distinct-root and finite-identity rules.

teaching_path.action: Challenge one unqualified slogan with a fresh counterexample and name the exact missing hypothesis.
teaching_path.why_valid: A counterexample falsifies the unconditional version while leaving the correctly qualified statement intact.
teaching_path.output: A reusable habit: condition first, conclusion second.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A familiar algebra slogan remains valid after its domain, leading coefficient, nonzero-polynomial or degree-bound condition is dropped.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Can you state one of the four rules without any condition and have it remain universally true?
misconceptions.repair: No. Write the hidden condition first, then apply the rule only inside that scope.

exit_task.prompt: Choose one of cancellation, degree, real-root count or finite agreement. State its qualified rule and one failure mode outside its hypotheses.

answer.summary: A correct answer names the governing condition and a counterexample to the unqualified version.
reasoning: Condition first; counterexample outside that condition.
answer.check: Verify that the counterexample violates the omitted hypothesis rather than the qualified rule.

questions.stem: A real polynomial r has degree at most two and r(0)=2, r(1)=3, r(2)=6. Show what is forced by the degree bound, then describe what changes if that bound is removed.

answer.summary: With degree at most two, r(x)=x^2+2 uniquely. Without the bound, r(x)=x^2+2+x(x-1)(x-2)h(x) for any real polynomial h.
reasoning: Check x^2+2 at the three inputs; the difference has three roots. A nonzero degree-at-most-two difference is impossible. Without the bound, factor all three roots from the difference.
answer.check: Substitute 0,1,2 and test h=1 as a distinct unbounded example.

difficulty.basis: Changed teaching anchor; difficulty is estimated for the authored case.

questions.stem: A real polynomial has zeros at -1,0,1, changes sign at ±1, and keeps the same nonzero sign on both sides of 0. If its degree is at most four, what multiplicities are forced before any scale condition is used?

answer.summary: The forced multiplicities are 1 at -1, 2 at 0, and 1 at 1.
reasoning: Translate sign change to odd multiplicity and no sign change to even multiplicity. The least positive choices already total four, so the degree bound leaves no room for larger multiplicities.
answer.check: The factor (x+1)x^2(x-1) flips sign at ±1 and not at 0.

difficulty.basis: Changed teaching anchor; difficulty is estimated for the authored case.

questions.stem: After factoring two allowed zeros from a candidate polynomial, an auxiliary factor g is known to satisfy g(-1)<0 and g(1)>0. Explain why a proposed quadratic g whose only allowed real zero in that interval would have to be a repeated zero cannot satisfy both sign conditions.

answer.summary: A quadratic with only one real zero has that zero with even multiplicity and therefore does not change sign across it; the opposite endpoint signs require a sign-changing real zero.
reasoning: Use continuity to force at least one real zero between -1 and 1. If the quadratic has only one real zero, its discriminant is zero and the root is double, so the sign does not switch. That contradicts the endpoint signs.
answer.check: Compare with (x-c)^2, which is nonnegative on both sides of c.

questions.stem: For G_t(x)=x(x+3)((t-2)x^2+(t+1)), derive every parameter value at which the degree or distinct real-zero pattern can change, then classify the parameter line.

answer.summary: Critical values are t=-1, 17/10, 2. For t<-1 and t>2 there are two distinct simple real zeros 0,-3. At t=-1 there are two distinct zeros with 0 of multiplicity 3. For -1<t<2 except 17/10 there are four distinct simple zeros. At t=17/10 there are three distinct zeros with -3 double. At t=2 the polynomial drops to degree 2 with simple zeros 0,-3.
reasoning: Factorization is already exposed. Degree drops when t-2=0. Extra real roots require (t+1)/(2-t)>0, with boundary t=-1. Collision with -3 occurs when (t+1)/(2-t)=9, giving t=17/10. Order the events and test each interval; refactor at each event.
answer.check: Choose t=0, t=19/10 and t=3 as interval checks, then substitute each exceptional t directly.

questions.stem: A 12 cm square sheet is cut by x cm corner squares to form an open box. A quadratic happens to match the true volumes at three chosen x-values. What information must be checked before treating that quadratic as the volume model?

answer.summary: Derive V(x)=x(12-2x)^2 from the geometry, state 0<x<6 for a non-degenerate box, then compare the candidate formula at an additional admissible x. Three matching rows alone do not identify the geometric law.
reasoning: The geometry fixes height x and base side 12-2x. The domain comes from positive dimensions. A finite set of matches can be shared by different polynomials, so a new domain-valid input or algebraic difference is needed.
answer.check: Check that the geometric volume remains nonnegative throughout 0<x<6 and compare a changed input.

questions.stem: Let H_b(x)=[x^2-(b+4)x+4b]/(x-b) on its original domain x≠b. Simplify on that domain, classify whether x=4 is a zero as b varies, and describe the polynomial extension.

answer.summary: H_b(x)=x-4 for x≠b. If b≠4, x=4 is an allowed zero; if b=4 it is excluded and H_b has no zero. The polynomial extension is x-4 on all real numbers.
reasoning: Factor the numerator as (x-b)(x-4), cancel only for x≠b, then test whether the candidate zero belongs to the original domain. Extension is a separate operation that fills the hole.
answer.check: At b=4 the simplified formula is zero at 4 but the original function is undefined there; this boundary case detects domain loss.

questions.stem: Four students claim: cancelling a common factor never changes a function; the written highest power is always the degree; a degree-n polynomial has n distinct real zeros; and agreement at three inputs proves two polynomials identical. Rewrite each as a correct conditional rule, then give one counterexample to an unqualified version.

answer.summary: Cancellation keeps values only on the original domain; degree is read after simplification and parameter checks; a nonzero degree-n polynomial has at most n distinct real zeros; finite agreement proves identity only when a suitable degree bound on the difference makes that many distinct roots impossible.
reasoning: Attach a domain condition to cancellation, a nonzero-leading-coefficient/simplification condition to degree, an at-most statement to real-root counting, and a degree bound to finite-data identity.
A counterexample such as (x-4)^2/(x-4) on x≠4 shows that cancellation alone does not restore the excluded point.
answer.check: For every repaired rule, remove its condition and verify that the supplied counterexample breaks the unqualified slogan.
